title: Free is wanting rightly
hook: the free person lives as they wish, which means wishing rightly
carry: same person, same day, different leash

segments.voice: Yesterday: at home here, Heracles at ease in every land. Your line was there is work for you to do. Did you say it once somewhere you'd rather not be? Day four hundred twenty-five.
screen: `AT HOME HERE — THERE IS WORK FOR YOU TO DO.`

segments.voice: Ask what freedom means, and a common answer is: doing what I want. No boss. No curfew. Nobody telling me what to do. It's a fine answer. Epictetus starts a long talk with almost the same definition, and then pulls a thread until the whole sweater comes apart. Book four, chapter one, is called On Freedom. He had a stake in the question: elsewhere in the Discourses he mentions the master he once had. Today: eleutheria.
screen: `FREEDOM: DOING WHAT I WANT?` → `ON FREEDOM, BOOK FOUR.` → `FREE IS WANTING RIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: First, the definition. Epictetus opens: the free person is the one who lives as they wish, who can't be forced, or blocked, or compelled. Second, the thread. Then he asks: does anyone wish to live in error? To be deceived, unjust, frightened, out of control? No one does. So anyone who lives that way is not living as they wish. And if they aren't living as they wish, by the first definition, they aren't free. Freedom turns out not to be about how many doors are open. It's about whether what you want is something you can actually have without betraying yourself. Third, the ladder. To make it vivid, he tells the story of a slave who longs to be freed. Once I'm free, he thinks, everything will be fine. He gets his freedom, and soon needs a patron to flatter for dinner. He climbs, saves, gets rich, maybe even rises to the senate. And at every rung he is serving someone, chasing someone's approval, more anxious than before. Epictetus says he's gone into a finer, fatter slavery. Fourth, the turn. Freedom, he concludes, is not won by getting everything you desire, but by removing the desire, the craving for what isn't yours to control. What's left is wanting what is in your own power, and holding the rest loosely. That isn't wanting nothing. It's wanting well. A person who wants to be honest today can be. A person who wants everyone to like them is at the mercy of everyone. Same person, same day. Different leash.
screen: `FREE: LIVING AS YOU WISH.` · `NO ONE WISHES TO LIVE IN ERROR.` · `THE FREED SLAVE'S LADDER.` · `NOT MORE DOORS: BETTER WANTS.` · then, large: `FREE IS WANTING RIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you want badly right now. A reply, a raise, someone's approval, a number on a scale. Hold it in mind. Now ask the Stoic question: which part of this is in my power? Maybe not the raise, but doing excellent work. Maybe not their reply, but how kindly you wrote. Let the want slide over onto that part, the part that's yours. Notice whether your shoulders change. Breathe with that smaller, steadier want. The bell holds the time.
Eleutheria. Greek for freedom: Epictetus' claim, On Freedom, that the free person lives as they wish, and the only way to do that is to wish for what is truly in their power.
Your line: same person, same day, different leash. Today, when a want starts pulling at you, move it one step, onto the piece that's yours to do. Day four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Stoic practice often means sorting a desire into the part that depends on oneself and the part that doesn't, and putting one's effort and hope on the first part.

he says it comes from removing the desire for what isn't in your power.
Epictetus says no one wishes to live deceived or unjust
so anyone living that way isn't living as they wish, and by his definition isn't free.
in his story, the freed slave finally finds peace in the senate
at every rung he's serving someone; Epictetus calls it a finer slavery.

fork.setup: you've just been freed. you have nothing, and a rich man offers you dinner every night if you'll flatter him. what does Epictetus' freed slave do?
options: takes the deal, and keeps climbing.
goes back to his old master.
fork.reveal: in the story he flatters, climbs, gets rich, even reaches the senate, and is never free, because his wants still belong to other people.

original.note: Greek: freedom; the subject of Discourses 4.1, Peri eleutherias, On Freedom.

trapdoor: what you thought: free means no one can tell you what to do.
what it means: Epictetus says the free person lives as they wish, which only works if they wish for what is in their power.
what a scholar hears: Epictetus had been enslaved himself; On Freedom turns the legal idea of a freed person into an inner one.
recall: the senator who kept going in

notes: Discourses 4.1.1–5: the definition of the free person (lives as he wishes, not compelled, hindered or forced) and the argument that no one wishes to live in error; paraphrased. Long's wording is close to 'He is free who lives as he wishes to live'; left unquoted.

Discourses 4.1.33–40: the slave who longs for freedom, then flatters a patron, then rises to the senate; 'a finer, fatter slavery' paraphrases Epictetus' phrasing. Confirm section numbers and the ladder's steps.
Discourses 4.1.175: freedom is not acquired by satisfying desire but by removing it; the script renders this as 'setting your desires straight'. Confirm this softer reading is fair.
On Freedom as the longest single discourse: standard claim; confirm.
